Neonatal Anegada ground iguanas emerge from their eggs after a relatively protracted incubation period, with eclosion typically occurring at 90 days [ab = 90 days] under stable conditions of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. Available records indicate that this incubation window can range from 79 to 93 days depending upon slight thermal fluctuations within the nest cavity. Upon emergence, hatchlings carry a modest wet weight at birth of 50 grams [Wwb = 50 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves invested in each offspring by the gravid female. This initial body mass is comparable to that reported for other West Indian Cyclura species of similar adult size, suggesting a conserved pattern of neonatal provisioning within the genus. The yolk-sac larva depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days after hatching, and the lecithotrophic phase persists until the onset of exogenous feeding, which typically begins within one to two weeks as the young iguanas start to consume tender vegetation and insect matter.

Under the controlled thermal regime of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], which approximates the average soil temperature in the limestone terraces of Anegada during the active season, juvenile females attain reproductive maturity and commence their first breeding at 1,095 days after hatching [tR = 1,095 days after hatching]. This corresponds to roughly three years of age, a relatively early onset of reproduction compared to larger-bodied Cyclura species such as Cyclura nubila, which may delay breeding until four or five years. The age at first reproduction is a critical life-history parameter for this critically endangered species, as it influences the population's capacity to recover from the severe demographic bottlenecks it has experienced. Field observations suggest that females nesting in deeper, more thermally buffered burrows may experience slightly accelerated growth and maturation, though the relationship between microhabitat temperature and developmental rate has not been rigorously quantified under natural conditions.

The reproductive output of the Anegada ground iguana, when considered under optimal conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], reveals a maximum annual rate of approximately 14 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 14 eggs per year]. This annual fecundity is achieved through the production of a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], each clutch typically containing between 12 and 16 eggs. The gravid female excavates a deep nest chamber within the sandy substrate to buffer the developing embryos from thermal extremes. The leathery-shelled eggs are deposited during the early wet season, ensuring that hatching coincides with the peak availability of new plant growth. This reproductive strategy represents a conservative approach relative to many smaller-bodied squamates, underscoring the metabolic and energetic constraints imposed by the species' large adult body size.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced within Cyclura pinguis, with the ultimate wet weight for females reaching 5,250 grams [Wwi = 5,250 grams], while males attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 7,750 grams [Wwi = 7,750 grams]. This disparity is evident by the time individuals reach their fifth year and is maintained throughout adulthood; the larger body mass of males is likely an adaptation for success in intrasexual combat during the breeding season, when males engage in vigorous head-butting and lateral displays to establish dominance hierarchies. Both sexes achieve these asymptotic masses after a protracted growth phase that extends over much of their adult lives. The slow growth trajectory, combined with delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output, characterizes Cyclura pinguis as a species with a typically K-selected life-history strategy, rendering it particularly vulnerable to the elevated adult mortality rates caused by introduced predators such as feral cats and dogs.

The maximum lifespan of the Anegada ground iguana under field conditions has been estimated at 30 years [am = 30 years], based on long-term mark-recapture studies conducted on a monitored population within the limestone forests of the Anegada Island at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. When considered at the standard reference temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], this longevity is consistent with the extended lifespans documented in other members of the genus Cyclura, which are among the longest-lived lizards in the Caribbean region. The species' demographic vulnerability is further compounded by the fact that senescence-related mortality generally becomes apparent only after the third decade of life, making the conservation of older, reproductively experienced individuals a priority for any recovery program.
